title: DNS Explained
pageTitle: DNS Explained · how names become addresses
description: A step-by-step look at how a domain name turns into an IP address.
subject: Domain Name System

intro.heading: What is DNS?
intro.lead: The internet's phone book. Your device asks a resolver for a name and gets back an address.
facts: the server that does the looking up for you
knows where every top-level domain lives
the server that owns the final answer
answers are kept for a while so lookups stay fast

spoof.title: Cache poisoning
spoof.text: If an attacker's fake answer arrives first, the resolver may cache it and send everyone to the wrong address.

whatsNext: How these are made, and more examples
footer: Sample topic built from one JSON file. Addresses are illustrative.

lessons.name: One lookup, start to finish
lessons.summary: Names are for people, addresses are for machines. DNS turns one into the other by asking a short chain of servers.

steps.title: Ask
steps.desc: You type a name. Your device asks the resolver for its address.

msgs.what: Asks the resolver for the IPv4 address (A record) of example.com.
msgs.why: The browser needs an IP address before it can connect. The resolver does the searching so the device does not.

steps.title: Find
steps.desc: The resolver asks the server that owns the name.

msgs.what: Asks the server that owns example.com for the name's A record.
msgs.why: The resolver has no cached answer. Only the authoritative server can give the final one.

msgs.what: Returns the A record: 93.184.215.14, valid for 3600 seconds.
msgs.why: This is the real answer. The lifetime tells the resolver how long it may reuse it.
notes: How many seconds the answer may be cached.

steps.title: Answer
steps.desc: The resolver passes the address back. The browser can now connect.

msgs.what: Hands the device the IP address it asked for.
msgs.why: The device never talks to the owning server. It trusts the resolver to pass the result back so it can connect.

lessons.name: Root, TLD, authoritative
lessons.summary: With an empty cache, the resolver starts at the root and follows referrals down the name.

steps.title: Root
steps.desc: The root doesn't know example.com, but knows who runs .com.

msgs.what: Asks a root server who handles example.com.
msgs.why: With an empty cache the resolver must start at the top. Root servers know where each top-level domain, such as .com, is run.

msgs.what: Replies with a referral: the name servers for .com.
msgs.why: The root does not hold the answer. It points the resolver one level down the name instead.

steps.title: TLD
steps.desc: The .com server points to the name's own servers.

msgs.what: Asks a .com server for example.com's address.
msgs.why: The resolver follows the referral. The TLD server knows which servers own each name under .com.

msgs.what: Replies with a referral to ns1.example.com, the name's own server.
msgs.why: The .com server still lacks the address. It sends the resolver to the server run by the name's owner.

steps.title: Owner
steps.desc: The authoritative server gives the real answer.

msgs.what: Asks ns1.example.com for the A record of example.com.
msgs.why: This server is the authority for the name, so it is the last stop in the chain.

msgs.what: Returns the A record for example.com with a 3600 second lifetime.
msgs.why: The authority gives the final answer. The resolver can cache it so later lookups skip the chain.

msgs.what: Gives the device the address the chain found.
msgs.why: The device is waiting on this answer. With it, the browser can open a connection.

lessons.name: Why the second lookup is instant
lessons.summary: Resolvers remember answers until their TTL runs out, so most lookups never leave your network.

steps.title: Hit
steps.desc: The resolver already has the answer and replies at once.

msgs.what: Asks the resolver for example.com again.
msgs.why: A repeat lookup shows the effect of caching. Nothing has changed except that the resolver now remembers.

msgs.what: Answers from the resolver's cache, with 3412 seconds of lifetime left.
msgs.why: The stored answer is still valid, so the resolver skips the chain. Lookups stay fast and the servers above see less traffic.

lessons.name: A fake answer wins the race
summary: An attacker who guesses a query's id can answer first, and the lie gets cached.
DNSSEC signatures and random ports make this much harder.

steps.title: Race
steps.desc: The resolver asks; the attacker floods it with forged answers.

msgs.what: Asks bank.com's authoritative server for its address, using query id 4711.
msgs.why: The resolver needs the real address. The id lets it match a reply to this query. An attacker would need to guess it.

msgs.what: Sends the resolver a fake answer pointing bank.com at 6.6.6.6.
msgs.why: Likely the attacker races the real reply. If it matches the query id and arrives first, the resolver may cache the lie.
